articles.headline: Buttigieg takes swipe at Trump administration amid FAA flight chaos
keyFacts: A nationwide FAA ground stop lasted over four hours Friday due to communications issues, causing flight delays and cancellations over the weekend.
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg questioned why the aviation system's built-in redundancies failed to prevent an outage of that scale.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the cause remains under investigation, including whether a contractor made an error or equipment failed.
body: DENVER — Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg took a swipe at the Trump administration’s handling of Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop, joking that he would help stranded travelers rebook flights as delays and cancellations continued.

I’ll begin with a public service announcement," Buttigieg told reporters in Denver. "I will be available in the hotel bar following the concert for anybody who needs to rebook their flights or get a refund per your rights."

He made the remark as the " What’s Next " conference wrapped up in Denver. The two-day gathering, hosted by Majority Democrats, brought leaders together to discuss the party’s direction after its midterm victories.
DEMS DESCEND ON DENVER TO SIZE UP 2028; WE ASKED WHO WANTS IN THE RACE

The FAA lifted the ground stop shortly after 8 p.m. Friday, more than four hours after it began, but flights remained delayed and canceled over the weekend. The agency cited safety concerns and serious air traffic control communications issues.

Buttigieg, who said he had no inside information about the cause of the ground stop, later questioned why the aviation system’s safeguards had not prevented an outage of that scale. He said he was watching the disruption as a traveler with a flight scheduled for Saturday.

"The system has many redundancies in it, so that normally, if there’s one point of failure, something else can catch it," he said. "It is not clear to me why that redundancy did not prevent an outage of this magnitude."
SCHUMER'S LEADERSHIP RIVAL REVEALS MAJOR SENATE RULE CHANGE HE'D PURSUE IF ELECTED

Meanwhile, Trump administration officials offered a mixed account of the failure. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the cause remained under investigation, including whether a contractor made an error or equipment failed.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin later said the stoppage was not caused by artificial intelligence or a cyberattack, but by aging infrastructure that needs to be updated. President Donald Trump told Fox News that the system had broken down because of its age.

Friday’s disruption was the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The first came in January 2023, when the FAA paused domestic departures for about 90 minutes because of an outage in its Notice to Air Missions system , which provides pilots with safety information.

The FAA said at the time it found no evidence of a cyberattack. Buttigieg ordered a review of that outage and directed the agency to report on what happened and recommend steps to prevent a recurrence.

articles.headline: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
keyFacts: Megaspeed said suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, who was linked to former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, left the company in August.
Megaspeed is suspected of providing Chinese firms backdoor access to Nvidia AI chips subject to US export restrictions.
Megaspeed launched an internal investigation, and US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month.
body: - Published
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.
Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".
The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced chips to China.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".
China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

articles.headline: No, the World Won’t Shut Down on Nov. 17. What the Blackout Rumors Get Wrong
keyFacts: FEMA and the FCC will conduct a nationwide Emergency Alert System test on Nov. 17.
Experts said viral social media rumors predicting an imminent blackout during the test are unfounded.
FEMA established a backup test date of Dec. 3 in case of emergencies or technical issues.
body: As global conspiracy theories go, this is a juicy one.

On Tuesday, Nov. 17, at around 2:20 p.m. ET, the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Federal Communications Commission are planning a test of the Emergency Alert System. That’s when all hell is supposed to break loose. At least, that’s what you might believe if you only rely on social media.

Coming just days after an abrupt and disruptive government-ordered shutdown of air travel in the US and technical issues that caused an unwelcome outage of widely used Microsoft workplace software, the test will be happening in an atmosphere of heightened anxiety.
More from CNET

Videos across Facebook, Instagram and TikTok have floated the theory that this emergency test signals a catastrophe is coming, potentially stemming from a cyberattack or a digital disruption that could knock out electricity, internet and other services. Many have started scrambling to buy emergency supplies, pointing to the need for a 90-day stockpile of food, water, cash and essential medicines in case hackers wipe out bank accounts and shut down the web.

Similar rumors have spread globally, as the governments of France, the UK and Canada have put renewed attention on the importance of households being able to survive a potential weather-related crisis or technological disaster.
How extreme have the conspiracy theories gotten? Some have cited a 2023 Simpsons episode as proof, which referenced a massive Nov. 17 blackout in Lisa’s future, even though it didn’t mention a year.

For Gen Xers and Boomers, this panic could feel familiar. Leading up to the year 2000, there were fears that a potential computer-related disaster, known as Y2K, would cause widespread chaos and disruption, based on the belief that older digital systems couldn’t handle the calendar change. The new year ended with only minor glitches, thanks to a significant global effort to update computer systems to avoid the bug.

Before we delve into the suspicions, let’s start with a bit of debunking: CNET spoke with multiple experts in disaster preparedness and cyberattacks, who all cautioned against letting our guard down. But remember that no federal agency or institution has mentioned a blackout. Unless hackers decide to take advantage of the hysteria already generated, there’s no reason to think Nov. 17 is any riskier than any other date.

Richard Mariano, a protective intelligence expert at Kronus Intelligence, who spent nearly three decades with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, said that people share all sorts of things that get picked up and go viral. “Then it creates panic where panic is not necessary,” he said.

Mariano said too many people are spreading fear rather than seeking the truth. “On every one of these social media posts that is suspect or has some form of conspiratorial edge to them: source it, source it, source it.”
What is happening on Nov. 17?

Next week’s nationwide Emergency Alert System, or EAS, is similar to the public tests Americans have experienced since 1963, when the Emergency Broadcast System replaced an older radio-based warning system called CONELRAD. In 1997, the Emergency Broadcast System was replaced by the EAS, part of FEMA’s Integrated Public Alert and Warning System, which broadcasts emergency alerts to any wireless device in the country, including phones, radios and televisions. The system was designed for the president to communicate with US households within 10 minutes of a national emergency.

The Nov. 17 test will consist of a nationwide EAS message issued by FEMA, noting that no public action is required. The test will include standard alert tones to support accessibility for those who are deaf or hard of hearing and should last about a minute. This time around, wireless emergency alerts will not be triggered on mobile phones, so don’t expect a notification on your cellphone. After the alert, programming should resume as normal on TV, radio and other broadcast channels.

Many equate the emergency system with threats of nuclear war, but it could also be used to alert people to a major weather event, a national cyberattack or even AMBER alerts at the local level (without a presidential message). So it’s natural there might be some anxiety.

“With this event simulating an activation of an emergency notification system, it would be a logical next step to worry about what happens if something bad happens during that test,” said Robby Winchester, chief global professional services officer at SpecterOps, a Virginia-based security company,

But, all in all, these system tests are routine. Local stations conduct a weekly test, and federal law requires a nationwide EAS test every three years. In addition to helping people get used to responding to alerts, the tests also allow the government to identify potential technical or operational issues it needs to fix before an actual emergency alert.

FEMA has a backup date of Dec. 3 in case it can’t perform it on Nov. 17 — which could happen if the agency is dealing with a real emergency or if there are technical issues. Representatives from the FCC and FEMA did not respond to a request for comment.
Why are blackout rumors spreading?

Another factor that helped spark conspiracy theories was a Pentagon order requiring military bases to stock enough supplies for 90 days without outside support. Dubbed “Fortress America,” the initiative memo (PDF) was released in late September but got more attention as the November date approached.

The timing of that memo coincided with the UK launching a campaign on Oct. 22 called Be Ready, urging citizens to keep enough supplies (PDF) such as water, food, medical kits and pet products to last at least three days. Other countries, including Japan, Sweden and about a dozen more, are also urging citizens to prepare for emergencies.

Still, the blackout rumor isn’t solely driven by government communications. Heightened global instability over the past few months has also played a major role. Just in the last month, the Federal Aviation Administration called a nationwide ground stop on all departing flights; a major Microsoft Outlook outage kept millions of people from working; PHP vulnerabilities exposed websites to hacking; and cyberattacks have targeted supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe.

On the financial side, Nvidia’s CEO scandal led to a stock plunge and fears of an AI bust, while Paraguay just experienced a major digital bank collapse that froze millions of accounts. The ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine have sparked national security concerns, and floods in Nepal and fires in Indonesia demonstrate the increased dangers of climate change.

Though there’s never been a nationwide power outage in the US (several regional outages have been triggered by overloaded lines and software bugs), The New York Times reports that there’s still no comprehensive plan for what to do if the country goes completely dark.
All the online chatter surrounding Nov. 17 has raised concerns that warnings of a potential cyberattack might inadvertently trigger one.

Winchester said that even though there’s no specific information indicating an imminent crisis, “it is common for attackers to use current events of all types to help with achieving successful attacks.” The upside? If people are being spurred by government notices and their anxiety over global instability to prepare emergency supplies, it could actually help in the event of a real threat or disaster.
How to prepare for a disruption (on any date)

Regardless of whether you buy into the Nov. 17 conspiracy theories, it doesn’t hurt to have some supplies at the ready, which could be useful in the event of a digital disruption or weather event, even if it doesn’t involve nuclear weapons or hackers.

“We live in a world where there are many threats to our communities, our families and ourselves,” said Philip Farina, chief advisor for Risky Business and a federal law enforcement veteran. “Understanding the basics of self-reliance is important. Even preparing for a residential fire, which is very common, can help to save lives and protect us better.”

You don’t need to buy enough for 90 days off the grid (and most of us can’t afford that), but it’s recommended that families have at least three days’ worth of food and supplies. Some of the basics listed on Ready.gov’s Build a Kit page include:
- A gallon of water per person per day
- Several days’ worth of nonperishable food
- A battery-powered or hand-crank radio to keep up with alerts
- A flashlight
- A first-aid kit
- Batteries
- A cellphone with a backup battery
- Optional: Pet supplies, sleeping bags, cash, a fire extinguisher and books or games for children

While warnings from governments can spark panic and distrust, they can be beneficial at a time when we’re so reliant on the internet and cell service, which can be easily disrupted. Mariano said it’s worth being prepared in the “old-fashioned ways.”

articles.headline: How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause
keyFacts: A study showed reduced human activity during 2020 COVID-19 lockdowns led to lower average fire activity.
Professor Jianghao Wang led the research team that published the study in Cell Reports Sustainability.
Human activities during dry weather conditions often combine with natural factors like wind to cause wildfires.
body: Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities.

Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people’s impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences.

A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.
Untangling humans from the weather

Fire doesn’t just happen anywhere. Although plenty of flammable materials exist in natural settings, not every place experiences wildfires. Some prairies burn almost every year, while many forests go without big fires for hundreds of years. Researchers explain these differences in terms of fire regimes, which are patterns describing when, how often, and how widely and intensely fires occur.

Weather is a major factor affecting fire regimes. An abundance of rain helps grow grass and trees that can become fuel for fires. Whether they do or not, however, can depend on the moisture inside plants; plants with enough moisture do not burn easily. By contrast, dry conditions make them more likely to catch fire. When a drought lasts, vegetation becomes increasingly flammable. Strong winds also accelerate fire growth and spread enormously.

Human activity often combines with weather conditions to cause fires. Even routine outdoor recreation can accidentally start a fire. More people venture outdoors during sunny, drier times of the year, increasing the risk of accidental fires when dry vegetation is more likely to be present.

articles.headline: Men weren’t always “bad at friendship”
keyFacts: Historian Tiffany Watt Smith said men historically formed deeply intimate friendships, challenging modern ideas about male emotional connection.
Changing nineteenth-century gender roles and twentieth-century anxieties about homosexuality reduced close male bonds, Smith stated.
Smith said friendship styles are not biologically fixed, meaning individuals can actively reshape and negotiate their relationships today.
body: Summer's Eve (1893) by Norwegian painter Halfdan Egedius. | Heritage Art/Heritage Images via Getty Images
The headlines may be dominated by artificial intelligence and electoral politics, but beneath it all, another debate constantly simmers, forever threatening to erupt.
I write, of course, of the great male friendship debate.

On one side: writers, journalists, and academics who fret over rising male loneliness , the emotional impact of friendless men on their partners , and the threat to society posed by atomized and isolated fellas. On the other: those who defend male friendships built around shared activities rather than heart-to-hearts.

These arguments often talk past each other. But the historian Tiffany Watt Smith offered me a way to think differently about both: that the gender roles undergirding the conversation are not nearly as fixed as they seem.

“I can definitely tell you that men in the past had much more intimate and romantic and involved friendships than we see today, for sure,” said Smith, who has published a number of books on the histories of friendship and emotions . “The idea that women are the kind of great experts in friendship is a really modern idea.”

I talked with Smith about Aristotle’s idea of the “perfect” friendship (it has to be between two dudes), how gendered notions of friendship inverted in the 19th century, and what men seeking deeper emotional connection from their buddies can learn from the past. You can hear that conversation and and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.

Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Smith, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
How do male friendships today compare to those of the past?

For thousands of years, it was really men who were considered the great experts in knowing how to form the highest kinds of friendships and the most intimate kind of bonds. And their friendships were considered the most meaningful and enduring and deep kind of friendships.

If you look back at David and Jonathan in the Bible or Achilles and Patroclus in the Iliad , you see these very dynamic, committed male friendships. When we look at the writings of Aristotle in the fourth-century BC, he’s talking about the deepest kind of friendship. He calls it the perfect friendship.

And this is between two men who he sees as soulmates. And he does say that there are other kinds of friendship, which are lesser friendships. He says you might make friends because it’s kind of convenient or because you enjoy doing the same kinds of things, or maybe you’re trying to help each other out. There’s a kind of quid pro quo-type of friendship. So he does see these kinds of friendship all around him. And he says women do those kinds of friendships.

One of the most famous pieces of writing about friendship ever is Michel de Montaigne’s essay “On Friendship.” Montaigne was a 16th-century essayist and lawyer, and he had this very, very close and committed friendship with another writer called La Boétie. And then after La Boétie died very unexpectedly, Montaigne wrote about their friendship and he said they had this kind of ideal friendship, the kind that Aristotle wrote about, this meeting of souls, and that this was rare and extraordinary.

And he was very explicit. He said, “Men can have these kinds of friendships.” But he very explicitly said, “Women are just incapable of having this kind of perfect friendship. They don’t have the kind of emotional stamina. They’re not clever enough. They’re not educated enough. Their souls aren’t strong enough, essentially, to withstand the complexities and difficulties of friendship.” So it’s a complete inversion from what we see today.

You used this word when you started: romantic. What did you mean by that? Was the Aristotelian conception of a perfect male friendship, was there a kind of romantic element in the way that we use the word romance?

Historians call this style of friendship “romantic friendship.” It doesn’t necessarily mean that they were having a physically active relationship or that they were having sex. They did see themselves as a partnership, and some of these male friends talked about themselves as married. This was a marriage of soul.
“Friendship is something that we have to negotiate on an individual basis. Each friendship is completely singular and we have to work out its rules.”

There’s a very important tombstone in Christ’s College in Cambridge, which commemorates these two doctors in the 16th century who basically lived their whole lives together. They traveled together, they did their research together and so on. And when they died, they were buried together. And the tomb does look like a conventional tomb between a husband and wife.

Now, we don’t know anything about their relationship in practice. I mean, the thing that really matters is the fact that this friendship, because it was commemorated as a friendship, the fact that it could be commemorated so vividly and publicly in such an extravagant way shows us that this is a culture that accepts and idealizes this kind of male friendship.
So how do we get from there to here?

Beginning in the 18th century and certainly by the 19th century, there’s a series of things that happen. One is that we get a distinction between the public space of the workplaces, cities are expanding, offices start to exist. The male sphere is fashioned as one of being in public, being a more rational sphere, and the female sphere starts to be connected with the home and intimacy and emotion.

Those ideas have been kind of floating around for a while, but they start to get really consolidated in the 19th century. And at the same time, a new ideal of femininity starts to emerge and it becomes a real sort of middle-class aspirational goal for women that they have very close friendships, almost as evidence that they can do all of these things.

Young girls in this era are taught a very particular style of friendship, which is, again, it’s very romantic. There’s lots of kissing and declarations of love and so on, but also it’s shown to be very committed. It’s very thoughtful, it’s very caring. And this is seen to be a kind of training ground for motherhood and for marriage.

At the end of the 19th century, we start to portray male friendships as kind of blundering and superficial and lacking in intimacy. And then of course, men carry on having close friendships, but by the beginning of the 20th century, another nail in the coffin, as it were, happens, which is that there’s a rise in understanding of homosexuality across Europe and America, and gay culture becomes much more visible.

In that moment, men become really anxious about having intimate and close relationships with other men. They’re worried about what that looks like and how that might be read. And that, in addition, leads to these anxieties about close male friendships.
If some guy is hearing this and is interested in having more fulfilling friendships, but he doesn’t know how to get there, where might he start?
The thing about history is that it shows us how much things have changed, but it also reminds us that things keep changing and can change again.

We’ve had this amazing history of these very romantic, intense, effusive male friendships. I think a lot of men probably would find that kind of overwhelming and unappealing as a model of friendship, but is there something in between? And one of the things I think that is important to remember is that we can make these changes and these shifts in style and these shifts in the patterns and our approaches to friendships.

One thing that I think it’s really worth listeners remembering is that since friendship has changed in the past, it can change again. There’s nothing biologically innate about the inability to make friends.
Which is freeing, the fact that friendship is not a fixed category for men or for women and that things can be what you want them to be. You’re not held back by some innate aspect of our biology.

I think that’s absolutely true. We get this notion that, well, men are sort of naturally worse at making friends or something, or they naturally have less kind of desire to connect with other people. That’s completely not true. The history of male friendships shows us that that is completely not true. So we can be released from that idea.

There isn’t an obvious, perfect, one-size-fits-all version of friendship. Friendship is something that we have to negotiate on an individual basis. Each friendship is completely singular and we have to work out its rules. What is my style of friendship? What is your style of friendship? How can we find something in the between so that we understand how to communicate and how not to hurt each other and how to build trust between each other?

articles.headline: Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit with major conflicts topping the agenda
keyFacts: Southeast Asian leaders opened their three-day annual summit in Manila on Sunday to discuss major global and regional conflicts.
Philippine President Marcos urged regional unity, stating that global problems are reshaping the region faster than any single country can respond.
Philippine officials said U.S. President Donald Trump will meet Marcos on Wednesday before both travel separately to an APEC summit in China.
body: MANILA, Philippines — Southeast Asian leaders opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila on Sunday for three days of talks, including dialogues with world leaders led by U.S. President Donald Trump, whose crucial trip to Asia could help boost his standing after his party’s defeat in the midterm elections.

The talks by the leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their expanded discussions with Asian and Western heads of state would focus on the world’s most troubling conflicts led by the war in the Middle East, according to drafts of post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press.

Trump is expected to land in Manila with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday afternoon, after the main ASEAN summit meetings have concluded and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. turns over the regional bloc’s rotating annual leadership to Singapore, Philippine officials said.

The ASEAN leaders are likely to renew calls for self-restraint and peaceful resolutions of conflicts, including longstanding disputes in the South China Sea and a civil war in Myanmar. They are also expected to press efforts to shield their economies and citizens from continuing fallout from intractable global conflicts.
“We reaffirmed our shared commitment to upholding international law, including the United Nations Charter,” the leaders’ draft statement says.

The statement also underlines the “importance of the peaceful resolution of disputes, upholding freedom of navigation and overflight and other lawful uses of the sea, including the right of transit passage in straits used for international navigation.”
Marcos said it’s crucial that despite the 11-nation regional bloc’s diversity, it has remained committed to remaining united in the face of headwinds.

“That commitment matters even more as the waters around us turn on shifting tides, geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, new technologies, climate change and transnational threats,” Marcos said in his opening remarks before ASEAN counterparts in a heavily secured convention center by Manila Bay.
Marcos warned problems across the world “are reshaping our region faster than any one country can respond to alone.”
But unity has been an elusive objective in ASEAN, a diverse bloc of democracies and authoritarian states, many of which are aligned with the United States or China.
ASEAN is known more for photo-ops projecting unity, cultural pomp and pageantry than for effectively dealing with the region’s conflicts, including Myanmar and the South China Sea.

Trump will join three key meetings late Tuesday, including a meeting of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue consisting of the United States, Japan, Australia and India, a grouping largely seen as a counterweight to China. He also will take part in a special summit with ASEAN leaders over cocktails, according to Philippine officials.

Trump will meet Wednesday with Marcos, who will receive him with a red-carpet welcome and a state luncheon at Manila’s presidential palace. They are expected to renew a commitment to their countries’ decades-old treaty alliance before flying separately to Shenzhen city in China for the APEC summit hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping.

“The short stop in Manila will help reassure allies and partners that they aren’t being forgotten before he jets off to Shenzhen to focus on meetings with Xi,” U.S.-based geopolitical analyst Greg Poling said.
He added that the midterm electoral setback suffered by Republicans will hound Trump in Asia.

“In China, the administration has been trying to lower expectations; there will be no substantive progress made between Trump and Xi,” Poling said. “With Trump politically weakened after the midterm drubbing here, it is likely that the Chinese side will be even less interested in making any compromises.”
China will be represented in the Manila summit by its premier, Li Qiang, who will meet ASEAN leaders on Monday but leave before Trump arrives, Philippine officials said.

articles.headline: LEO gets a birthday bash, 75 years after clocking in
keyFacts: Cambridge's Centre for Computing History is hosting the LEO@75 event on Saturday, November 28, marking 75 years of business computing.
LEO was an early computer based on EDSAC that ran its first commercial application in 1951.
The event features film screenings, historical displays, and coding activities, with admission supporting the museum charity.
body: Business computing turns 75 this month, and Cambridge's Centre for Computing History is throwing a party for LEO, the machine that helped start it all.
The LEO@75 event takes place on Saturday, November 28, from 10am to 5pm, with film screenings, historical displays, and hands-on activities for children.

The Register has written about the Centre for Computing History a few times. It's an interactive computer museum just off Coldhams Lane in Cambridge, and back in 2018 it won National Lottery funding to help it "preserve, archive and digitise a range of LEO Computers artefacts, documents and personal memories."

Admission supports the museum charity, with student and concession tickets at £10 and family tickets starting at £15. As well as stuff for the grown-ups, including a film screening, it will include events for smaller children (5-7) and a Python coding event for older (12-16) kids.

Regular readers might recall our story about the Lyons Electronic Office back in 2021, celebrating its 70th anniversary. The Reg also published an obituary for Mary Coombs, the first female commercial programmer the following year. Coombs started programming LEO in 1952. Both stories offer more on the machine and the people behind it.

LEO was an early computer, but from three-quarters of a century away, it's easy to miss just how early. Its design was based on Cambridge University's EDSAC, developed by a team led by the late, great Sir Maurice Wilkes. The Reg mentioned EDSAC in our obituary for Wilkes, and went into more detail for his centenary in 2013 . It also crops up in our Geek's Guide to Cambridge .

The design of EDSAC was directly inspired by John von Neumann's famous, and incomplete, "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" – which The Reg talked about in 2011 . The draft report was circulated in 1945, based on the proposal for EDVAC, four years before the hardware was delivered. That was also the year John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert completed its predecessor, ENIAC. In its original form, ENIAC was programmed by setting switches and reconnecting cables; EDVAC, by contrast, was designed to store its instructions in memory.

The report set out what's now called the "von Neumann architecture." Wilkes and Douglas Hartree drew on those ideas in developing EDSAC, LEO's immediate forerunner and one of the world's earliest practical stored-program computers. The first working electronic stored-program machine was the Manchester "Baby," the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, which ran its first program in 1948 .

EDSAC ran its first program in May 1949 – a few months before the delivery of BINAC, Eckert and Mauchly's first stored-program machine. LEO ran its first commercial application in 1951. That was also the year the US Census Bureau took delivery of Eckert and Mauchly's UNIVAC I . ®

articles.headline: Trump Posts More Than 40 Images Of Latest Renovation Obsession Amid Heated Legal Battle
keyFacts: Donald Trump posted dozens of photos showing damage at Washington's East Potomac Park while advocating to redevelop its golf course.
Preservation groups filed an emergency request to block the closure, prompting a judge to express skepticism over administration motives.
The park is slated to close Sunday, pending a ruling from the judge.
body: President Donald Trump posted dozens of images on Saturday of Washington, D.C.’s East Potomac Park and Golf Links, an area he has dubbed “Trash Island,” amid a legal battle to close the park and redevelop the golf course.

“Trash Island is currently the Worst Golf Course anywhere in the World, but the Department of the Interior is going to make it into the Best Golf Course anywhere in the World,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in a post topping 300 words.
The images Trump posted showed flooding, damaged fences and various debris. In all, the president shared 44 photos, though some were the same photos posted twice.

On Friday, U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes expressed skepticism over the administration’s motives for its plans to close the park and golf course, after preservation groups filed an emergency request to block the closure. The park is slated to close Sunday, pending a ruling from Reyes, who Trump previously called a “crazed lunatic” and suggested “may be insane?”

The administration has argued the closure needs to happen due to safety concerns, and because the trust that operates the golf course will not be operating it anymore. The trust’s lease for the golf course was terminated by Trump’s Department of the Interior.
Federal officials have insisted that they are not closing the park because of designs on overhauling the golf course and turning it into, as he has put it, a “world class” facility.
Last month, Reyes temporarily blocked the administration from cutting down more trees at the site after it felled hundreds — something officials also said was unrelated to Trump’s renovation plans.

Nevertheless, Trump in his Saturday post accused Reyes of not wanting his administration to “quickly and inexpensively fix up” the golf course. He added that he believed she would ultimately come around and rule in his favor.
“Trash Island, after years of laughter and scorn, will evolve into something very special, something which the Judge will be able to take great pride in seeing!” he wrote.
